contact_edits.before: What he's collaborating with is the Anschluss, which the production does its level best to make terrifying without much help from the text. (What's there is real enough; it's just that so much is left out.) The theatre itself becomes the Salzburg concert-hall in which the Trapp Family Singers' effect their trompe l'oeil transformation into the Trapp Family Refugees, and there are indeed storm troopers in the aisles, though they're still not as scary as the nuns. But no staging has the technical resources to compete with the film here, or in what follows. The production does add a new dark touch: Max, left behind, gets arrested. But we're given no time to ponder what might happen to him (or to thousands of others); we're whisked on to an uplifting finale. The Sisters reprise that meaningless mountain-climbing song, which is You'll Never Walk Alone minus the soul, in the bottom half of the stage, while in the top half the Trapps on their Alp are seen obeying the injunction, while fixing the audience with a collective grin that's pure postcard kitsch. It's certainly in keeping with the spirit of the show, if not with the general handsomeness of the production. It's just that after Cabaret and, in its way, The Producers, a (literally) escapist musical about Nazism seems -- I was going to say dim-witted but I'll settle for myopic. - The Sound of Music runs until Jan. 11. Call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com for information.
